nodes.name: Frame (continuous frame)
nodes.statement: A frame on $H$ is a map $f:X\mapsto H$ for which $\left\langle \phi, f\left( x\right) \right\rangle$ is weakly measurable with respect to $\mu$ for all $\phi \in H$ and for which there exist constants $0<A\leq B$ such that $$ A\left\Vert \phi \right\Vert ^{2}\leq \int_{X}\left\vert \left\langle \phi,f\left( x\right) \right\rangle \right\vert ^{2}d\mu \left( x\right) \leq B\left\Vert \phi \right\Vert ^{2} $$
nodes.statement_short: A weakly measurable map $f:X\to H$ whose squared coefficient integral is two-sided bounded by $\|\phi\|^2$.
nodes.origin_citation: Ali, Antoine & Gazeau 2014; Ali et al. 1993; Heil 1989; Rahimi et al. 2006
differentia: $\left\langle \phi, f\left( x\right) \right\rangle$ is weakly measurable with respect to $\mu$ for all $\phi \in H$

there exist constants $0<A\leq B$ such that $$ A\left\Vert \phi \right\Vert ^{2}\leq \int_{X}\left\vert \left\langle \phi,f\left( x\right) \right\rangle \right\vert ^{2}d\mu \left( x\right) \leq B\left\Vert \phi \right\Vert ^{2}

nodes.name: Frame bounds and Parseval frame
nodes.statement: The constants $A,B$ are called the \emph{frame bounds} of $f$, and if $A=B=1,$ then $f$ is called a \emph{Parseval frame}. Specifically, a Parseval frame $f$  satisfies $$\int_{X}\left\vert \left\langle \phi,f\left( x\right) \right\rangle \right\vert ^{2}d\mu \left( x\right) = \left\Vert \phi \right\Vert ^{2} $$ for all $\phi \in H$.
nodes.statement_short: A Parseval frame is a frame with $A=B=1$, i.e. the coefficient integral reproduces $\|\phi\|^2$ exactly.

nodes.name: Adjugation $\ad_A$
nodes.statement: For every $A\in \GL(H)$, let the map $\ad_A:\GL(H)\mapsto \GL(H)$ be defined $$\ad_A(B) = ABA^*.$$ We say that $\ad_A(B)$ is the \emph{adjugation} of $B$ by $A$.

nodes.name: Adjugacy relation $\sim$
nodes.statement: We define the relation $\sim$ on $\GL(H)$ by $B\sim B^\prime$ if and only if $\ad_A(B)=B^\prime$ for some $A\in\GL(H)$.

nodes.name: Adjugacy classes
nodes.statement: The equivalence classes in $\GL(H)$ induced by $\sim$ are called \emph{adjugacy classes}.

nodes.name: Projection $\rho(A)=AA^*$
nodes.statement: Next, we define the projection \begin{equation} \rho:\GL(H)\mapsto \GL^+(H), \quad \rho(A)=AA^*, \end{equation} which is important in the proof of the following lemma establishing an important relationship between $\GL^+(H)$ and $\GL(H)$.
nodes.statement_short: The map sending an invertible operator $A$ to the positive operator $AA^*$.

nodes.name: The Banach space $J = L^\infty(X,H)$
nodes.statement: We first define the Banach space $J$ to be \begin{equation} J = L^\infty(X, H) = \left\{f:X\mapsto H: \sup_{x\in X} \|f(x)\|_H <\infty\right\}, \end{equation} equipped with the norm \[ \|f\|_J = \sup_{x\in X} \|f(x)\|_H. \] where the subscripts indicate the space in which the norm is applied.
nodes.statement_short: $J$ is the Banach space of essentially bounded $H$-valued maps on $X$ with the sup norm.

nodes.name: The frame spaces $F$ and $F_0$
nodes.statement: In addition, we define the spaces \begin{align} F &= \{f\in J: f \mbox{ is a frame}\} \\ F_0 &= \{f\in F: f \mbox{ is Parseval}\}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $F$ is the set of bounded frames in $J$ and $F_0\subset F$ its subset of Parseval frames.
differentia: F &= \{f\in J: f \mbox{ is a frame}\}

nodes.name: Frame operator map $S:F\mapsto \GL^+(H)$
nodes.statement: Define the ``frame operator map'' $S:F\mapsto \GL^+(H)$ such that $S(f)$ is the frame operator of $f$.

nodes.name: Parseval projection $T(f)=S(f)^{-1/2}f$
nodes.statement: Define the projection \begin{equation} T:F\mapsto F_0, \quad T(f) = S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $T$ rescales a frame by the inverse square root of its frame operator to make it Parseval.

nodes.name: Transversal $\Fbar_0$ of $F_0/U(H)$
nodes.statement: Let $\Fbar_0$ be a fixed transversal of the orbit space $F_0/U(H)$, so that $\Fbar_0$ is a maximal set of unitarily inequivalent Parseval frames on $H$.
nodes.genus: fixed transversal of the orbit space $F_0/U(H)$
differentia: a maximal set of unitarily inequivalent Parseval frames on $H$

nodes.name: Projection maps $U$ and $\sigma$
nodes.statement: We therefore define the projection maps \begin{equation} U:F_0\mapsto U(H) \mbox{ and } \sigma:F_0\mapsto \Fbar_0 \mbox{ such that } f = U(f)\sigma(f) \mbox{ for all } f\in F_0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $U$ and $\sigma$ extract the unitary and transversal factors of the unique factorization $f=U(f)\sigma(f)$.
differentia: f = U(f)\sigma(f) \mbox{ for all } f\in F_0.

nodes.name: The maps $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$
nodes.statement: First, we define the maps \begin{align} \zeta:\GL(H)\times\Fbar_0\mapsto F, \quad &\zeta(A, f) = Af \\ \zeta^+:\GL^+(H)\times F_0\mapsto F, \quad &\zeta^+(A, f) = Af. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ act an operator on a (transversal or Parseval) frame to produce a general frame.

nodes.name: Fiber bundle and principal fiber bundle
nodes.statement: Let $E_1$ and $B$ be topological spaces. A topological space $E$ is a called \emph{fiber bundle} with base space $B$ and fiber $E_1$ if there exists a \emph{projection} or continuous surjection $\pi:E\mapsto B$ that satisfies the \emph{local triviality condition}: For every $x\in E$, there is an open neighborhood $U\subseteq B$ about $\pi(x)$ and a homeomorphism $\theta:\pi^{-1}(U)\mapsto U\times E_1$ such that \[ \pi(x) = (\pi_U\circ\theta)(x), \quad\forall x\in \pi^{-1}(U), \] where $\pi_U:U\times E_1\mapsto U$ is the natural projection from the product space $U\times E_1$ to the first factor $B$. If the fiber $E_1$ is a principal homogeneous space under the action of a group $G$, then $E$ is called a \emph{principal fiber bundle} with \emph{structure group} $G$.
nodes.statement_short: A fiber bundle is a space with a continuous surjection onto a base that is locally a product with the fiber; principal if the fiber is a principal homogeneous $G$-space.
nodes.genus: topological space $E$ with a projection $\pi:E\mapsto B$
differentia: there exists a \emph{projection} or continuous surjection $\pi:E\mapsto B$
there is an open neighborhood $U\subseteq B$ about $\pi(x)$ and a homeomorphism $\theta:\pi^{-1}(U)\mapsto U\times E_1$ such that \[ \pi(x) = (\pi_U\circ\theta)(x)

nodes.name: Projection maps $\pi_1$ and $\pi_2$
nodes.statement: Finally, we define the continuous projection maps \begin{align*} \pi_1:\GL(H)\times F_0\mapsto \GL(H), \quad &\pi_1(A, f) = A \\ \pi_2:\GL(H)\times F_0\mapsto F_0, \quad &\pi_2(A, f) = f. \end{align*}

nodes.name: The space $F_1 = \GL(H)f_{10}$
nodes.statement: Proceeding, we fix some Parseval frame $f_{10}\in\Fbar_0$ and define the space \begin{equation} F_1 = \GL(H)f_{10} = \{Af_{10}: A\in \GL(H)\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $F_1$ is the $\GL(H)$-orbit of a fixed Parseval frame $f_{10}$, which will serve as the fiber of $F$.

nodes.name: Projection map $T_1:F\mapsto F_1$
nodes.statement: Consequently, we define the projection map \begin{equation} T_1:F\mapsto F_1, \quad T_1(f) = \pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f))f_{10}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: The map $\theta:F_1\mapsto\GL(H)$
nodes.statement: Next, we define the map \begin{equation} \theta:F_1\mapsto\GL(H), \quad \theta(f) = \pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f)). \end{equation}

nodes.name: The lifted map $\theta_*$
nodes.statement: The bijection $\theta$ may be lifted to the map \begin{equation} \theta_*:F_1\times\Fbar_0\mapsto F, \quad \theta_*(f_1, f_0) = \zeta(\theta(f_1), f_0). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\theta_*$ lifts $\theta$ to a map from the product $F_1\times\Fbar_0$ onto $F$.

nodes.name: The Banach space $J_1 = L^1(X,H)$
nodes.statement: We first define the Banach space \[ J_1 = L^1(X, H) \] equipped with the norm \[ \|f\|_{J_1} = \int_X \|f(x)\|_H\,d\mu(x). \]

nodes.name: Frame matrix
nodes.statement: if $X=\left\{ 1,\ldots ,n\right\} $ where $n\geq m>0,$ then we will say that an $n\times m$ matrix $T$ is a \emph{frame matrix}, or simply a \emph{frame} if the context is understood, if the set of columns obtained by Hermitian transposing its rows are a frame.  Moreover, given a frame $\left\{ f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}\right\} \subset \mathbb{C}^{m},$ we will say that it generates the frame matrix $T$ if the rows of $T$ are  $f_{j}^{\ast },$ $j=1,\ldots ,n.$
nodes.statement_short: An $n\times m$ matrix whose conjugate-transposed rows form a frame in $\mathbb{C}^m$.
differentia: the set of columns obtained by Hermitian transposing its rows are a frame

nodes.name: The matrix set $M_{\Sigma }$
nodes.statement: if we define $M_{\Sigma }$ to be the set of $n\times m$ matrices whose rows have at most a single non-zero entry and whose columns are unit vectors in $\mathbb{C}^{n}$, then a choice of base space $\bar{F}_{0}$ for $X=\left\{1,\ldots n\right\} $ over $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ is a maximally non-unitary subset of $M_{\Sigma }$ (there are matrices in $M_{\Sigma }$ that are unitarily equivalent).
nodes.statement_short: $M_\Sigma$ collects $n\times m$ matrices with at most one nonzero entry per row and unit columns; a maximally non-unitary subset of it serves as base space.
differentia: whose rows have at most a single non-zero entry
whose columns are unit vectors in $\mathbb{C}^{n}$

nodes.name: Canonical dual frame
nodes.statement: The canonical dual frame of $f(x)$ is $\tilde{f}(x) = S^{-1}f(x)$. It is also sometimes referred to as ``the dual frame.''

nodes.name: Frame operator $S=T^*T$ (finite-dimensional)
nodes.statement: Moreover, $S=T^{\ast }T$ is a positive matrix called the \emph{frame operator} for $\left\{ f_{1},\ldots ,f_{n}\right\} $.

nodes.name: The map $\pi_1^2$
nodes.statement: By $\pi_1^2$, we mean $\pi_1^2(A, f) = A^2$.

nodes.name: Frame characterization via the frame operator
nodes.statement: A map $f:X\mapsto H$ is a frame if and only if the operator $S:H\mapsto H$ (given by Eq. \ref{S}) is bounded and has bounded inverse. If $f$ is a frame, then its frame bounds are given by $A=\frac{1}{\|S^{-1}\|_H}$ and $B=\|S\|_H$.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is a frame exactly when its frame operator is invertible with bounded inverse, and the frame bounds are $1/\|S^{-1}\|$ and $\|S\|$.
conclusions: A map $f:X\mapsto H$ is a frame if and only if the operator $S:H\mapsto H$ (given by Eq. \ref{S}) is bounded and has bounded inverse.
its frame bounds are given by $A=\frac{1}{\|S^{-1}\|_H}$ and $B=\|S\|_H$.

nodes.name: Existence of a dual frame (Reconstruction Property)
nodes.statement: Let $f:X\mapsto H$ be a frame. Then, there exists a frame $\tilde{f}:X\mapsto H$ such that for all $\phi\in H$, \begin{equation} \phi = \int_X\brak{\phi, f(x)} \tilde{f}(x)\,d\mu(x). \tag{Reconstruction Property} \end{equation} Any such $\tilde{f}$ is called a \emph{dual frame} of $f$. Moreover, if $f$ is the frame operator of $f$, then the map $\tilde{f}:X\mapsto H$ defined by $\tilde{f}(x)=S^{-1}f(x)$ is a dual frame of $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Every frame admits a dual frame giving exact reconstruction, and $S^{-1}f$ is one such dual.
conclusions: there exists a frame $\tilde{f}:X\mapsto H$ such that for all $\phi\in H$, \begin{equation} \phi = \int_X\brak{\phi, f(x)} \tilde{f}(x)\,d\mu(x)
the map $\tilde{f}:X\mapsto H$ defined by $\tilde{f}(x)=S^{-1}f(x)$ is a dual frame of $f$

nodes.name: $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are continuous bijections
nodes.statement: The maps $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are continuous bijections.
conclusions: The maps $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are continuous bijections.

nodes.name: $\theta_*$ is a bijection with inverse $(T_1,\sigma\circ T)$
nodes.statement: The map $\theta_*$ is a bijection and has inverse \[ \theta^{-1}(f) = (T_1(f), \sigma\circ T(f)). \]
nodes.statement_short: $\theta_*$ identifies $F$ with $F_1\times\Fbar_0$, its inverse being the pair of projections $T_1$ and $\sigma\circ T$.
conclusions: The map $\theta_*$ is a bijection
\theta^{-1}(f) = (T_1(f), \sigma\circ T(f))

nodes.name: $F$ is a principal fiber bundle in the topology of $J_1$
nodes.statement: The map $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$. Moreover, $F$ is a principal fiber bundle with base space $\Fbar_0$, fiber $F_1$, and structure group $\GL(H)$ in the topology of $J_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Main result: in the $L^1$ topology, $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous and the space of frames is a principal $\GL(H)$-bundle over $\Fbar_0$.
assumptions: Suppose that $F\subset J_1$. That is, suppose that all frames (in $J$) on $H$ are integrable.
Suppose $\Fbar_0$ is a continuous transversal of $F/\GL(H)$.
conclusions: The map $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$
$F$ is a principal fiber bundle with base space $\Fbar_0$, fiber $F_1$, and structure group $\GL(H)$ in the topology of $J_1$

nodes.name: $\GL(H)\subset \GL(J)$
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\GL(H)$ and $f\in J$ and define the action of $A$ on $f$ by \[ (Af)(x) = A[f(x)]. \] Then $\GL(H)\subset \GL(J)$. That is, $A$ and $A^{-1}$ are bounded on $J$.
nodes.statement_short: The pointwise action of an invertible operator on $H$ is invertible and bounded on $J=L^\infty(X,H)$.
assumptions: define the action of $A$ on $f$ by \[ (Af)(x) = A[f(x)]
conclusions: $\GL(H)\subset \GL(J)$
$A$ and $A^{-1}$ are bounded on $J$

nodes.name: Linear deformation of a frame and its frame operator
nodes.statement: Let $f\in F$ and $A\in\GL(H)$. Then $Af\in F$ and the frame operator of $Af$ is $$S(Af) = \ad_A(S(f)) = AS(f)A^*.$$
nodes.statement_short: Acting on a frame by $A\in\GL(H)$ gives a frame whose frame operator is the adjugation $AS(f)A^*$.
conclusions: $Af\in F$
the frame operator of $Af$ is $$S(Af) = \ad_A(S(f)) = AS(f)A^*

nodes.name: Regularity of the $\GL(H)$ action on orbits
nodes.statement: Consider any $f\in F$ and $A\in\GL(H)$. Then $Af=f$ if and only if $A=I$. In other words, the action of $\GL(H)$ is regular on each orbit in $F/\GL(H)$.
nodes.statement_short: Only the identity operator fixes a frame, so $\GL(H)$ acts regularly on each orbit.
conclusions: $Af=f$ if and only if $A=I$
the action of $\GL(H)$ is regular on each orbit in $F/\GL(H)$

nodes.name: Parseval-preserving operators are exactly the unitaries
nodes.statement: Let $f\in F_0$ and $A\in\GL(H)$. Then, $Af\in F_0$ if and only if $A\in U(H)$.
conclusions: $Af\in F_0$ if and only if $A\in U(H)$

conclusions: The map $S:F\mapsto\GL^+(H)$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$.

conclusions: The map $T:F\mapsto F_0$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$.

conclusions: The map $U:F_0\mapsto U(H)$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$.

nodes.name: Parseval frames combine over a product measure space
nodes.statement: If $F_{j}\left( x\right) $, $j\in \mathbb{Z}$, are Parseval frames from a measure space $\left( X,\mu \right) $ into a separable Hilbert space $H,$ and if $\alpha _{j}\left( y\right) ,\ \ j\in \mathbb{Z}$, is an orthonormal subset of $L^{2}\left( Y,\nu \right) $ for a measure space $\left( Y,\nu \right) ,$ then $$ K\left( x,y\right) =\sum_{j=-\infty }^{\infty }\alpha _{j}\left( y\right) F_{j}\left( x\right) $$ is a Parseval frame on $H$ over the product measure space of $X$ and $Y.$
nodes.statement_short: An orthonormal-function-weighted superposition of Parseval frames is a Parseval frame on the product measure space.
assumptions: $F_{j}\left( x\right) $, $j\in \mathbb{Z}$, are Parseval frames from a measure space $\left( X,\mu \right) $ into a separable Hilbert space $H,$
$\alpha _{j}\left( y\right) ,\ \ j\in \mathbb{Z}$, is an orthonormal subset of $L^{2}\left( Y,\nu \right) $ for a measure space $\left( Y,\nu \right) ,$
conclusions: K\left( x,y\right) =\sum_{j=-\infty }^{\infty }\alpha _{j}\left( y\right) F_{j}\left( x\right) $$ is a Parseval frame on $H$ over the product measure space of $X$ and $Y.

nodes.name: Analysis, Synthesis, and Frame Operators
nodes.statement: Let $f:X\mapsto H$ be a frame. The operator defined by \begin{equation} V:H\mapsto L^2(X), \quad (V\phi)(x) = \brak{\phi, f(x)}_H \tag{Analysis Operator} \end{equation} is well-defined, bounded, and has a bounded inverse. The adjoint of $V$ is given by \begin{equation} V^*:L^2(X)\mapsto H, \quad V^*\alpha = \int_X \alpha(x)f(x)\,d\mu(x), \tag{Synthesis Operator} \end{equation} where convergence of the integral is taken in $H$. Finally, the operator defined by \begin{equation} S:H\mapsto H, \quad S\phi = V^*V\phi = \int_X\brak{\phi, f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x) \tag{Frame Operator} \end{equation} is positive, self-adjoint, bounded, and has a bounded inverse.
nodes.statement_short: Every frame determines a bounded invertible analysis operator $V$, its adjoint synthesis operator $V^*$, and a positive invertible frame operator $S=V^*V$.
conclusions: V:H\mapsto L^2(X), \quad (V\phi)(x) = \brak{\phi, f(x)}_H \tag{Analysis Operator} \end{equation} is well-defined, bounded, and has a bounded inverse
The adjoint of $V$ is given by \begin{equation} V^*:L^2(X)\mapsto H, \quad V^*\alpha = \int_X \alpha(x)f(x)\,d\mu(x)
S:H\mapsto H, \quad S\phi = V^*V\phi = \int_X\brak{\phi, f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x) \tag{Frame Operator} \end{equation} is positive, self-adjoint, bounded, and has a bounded inverse

conclusions: the orbit space $\GL(H)/U(H)$ is in one-one correspondence with $GL^+(H)$

$F$ is a principal fiber bundle with base space $\Fbar_0$, fiber $F_1$, and structure group $\GL(H)$

nodes.name: Form of every finite Parseval frame over $\mathbb{C}^m$
nodes.statement: It follows that every Parseval frame $\left\{ g_{1},\ldots, g_{n}\right\} $ over $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ is of the form $$ \left[ \begin{array}{c} g_{1}^{\ast } \\ \vdots        \\ g_{m}^{\ast } \\ \vdots        \\ g_{n}^{\ast } \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{ccc} u_{11} & \ldots  & u_{1m} \\ \vdots  & \ddots  & \vdots \\ u_{m1} & \ldots  & u_{mm} \\ \vdots  & \ddots  & \vdots \\ u_{n1} & \ldots  & u_{nm} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{ccc} v_{11} & \ldots  & v_{1m}  \\ \vdots  & \ddots  & \vdots  \\ v_{m1} & \ldots  & v_{mm} \end{array} \right] $$ where the first matrix is the first $m$ columns of $V^{\ast }.$ This is essentially the same as the construction in \cite{casazza2008classes} and also in \cite{casazza2001uniform}.
nodes.statement_short: Every finite Parseval frame in $\mathbb{C}^m$ factors as the first $m$ columns of a unitary times an $m\times m$ unitary.
assumptions: For an $m$-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ and a finite index set $X=\left\{ 1,\ldots ,n\right\} ,$ where $m\leq n,$
If we define $$g_{j}=S^{-1/2}f_{j}$$ then $\left\{ g_{1},\ldots ,g_{n}\right\} $ is a \emph{Parseval frame} in $\mathbb{C}^{m},

nodes.name: Parseval frames are exactly those with $S=I$
nodes.statement: It follows that a map $f:X\mapsto H$ is a Parseval frame if and only if its frame operator is the identity operator $S=I$.

nodes.name: Proof that $\sim$ is an equivalence relation
nodes.statement: Let $B\in\GL(H)$. Clearly, $\ad_I(B)=IBI^*=B$, so that $B\sim B$. Thus, $\sim$ is reflexive. Given $B,B^\prime\in\GL(H)$, suppose $B\sim B^\prime$. That is, $ad_A(B)=ABA*=B^\prime$ for some $A\in\GL(H)$. Then, \[ \ad_{A^{-1}}(B^\prime) = A^{-1}B^\prime (A^{-1})^* = A^{-1}ABA^*(A^*)^{-1} = B. \] Thus, $B^\prime\sim B$, and hence $\sim$ is symmetric. Finally, suppose $B\sim B^\prime$ and $B^\prime\sim B^{\prime\prime}$. Thus, $\ad_A(B)=ABA^*=B^\prime$ and $\ad_{A^\prime}(B^\prime)=A^\prime B^\prime (A^\prime)^*=B^{\prime\prime}$ for some $A,A^\prime\in\GL(H)$. Then, \[ \ad_{A^\prime A}(B) = A^\prime AB(A^\prime A)^* = A^\prime (ABA^*)(A^\prime)^* = A^\prime B^\prime (A^\prime)^* = B^{\prime\prime}. \] Thus, $B\sim B^{\prime\prime}$, and hence $\sim$ is transitive.
nodes.statement_short: Verify reflexivity with $A=I$, symmetry with $A^{-1}$, and transitivity with the composite $A^\prime A$.

nodes.name: Proof that $\GL^+(H)$ is an adjugacy class
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\GL(H)$ and $B\in\GL^+(H)$. For any $\phi\in H$, we have \[ \brak{\ad_A(B)\phi, \phi} = \brak{ABA^*\phi, \phi} = \brak{BA^*\phi, A^*\phi}\geq 0, \] where the inequality holds since $A^*\phi\in H$ and $B$ is positive. Thus, $\ad_A(B)$ is positive, so that $GL^+(H)$ is closed under adjugation. Let $B,C\in\GL^+(H)$. Since $B,C$ are positive, then $B=SS^*$ and $C=TT^*$ for some $S,T\in\GL(H)$. There exists $A\in\GL(H)$ such that $T=AS$. We have \[ \ad_A(B) = ABA^* = ASS^*A^* = (AS)(AS)^* = TT^* = C. \] Thus, $B\sim C$. Ergo, $\GL^+(H)$ is an adjugacy class.
nodes.statement_short: Show closure of positivity under adjugation, then connect any two positive operators via their square-root factorizations.

nodes.name: Proof that $\GL(H)/U(H)$ corresponds to $\GL^+(H)$
nodes.statement: Since every positive operator $B\in\GL^+(H)$ can be written in the form $B=AA^*$ with $A\in\GL(H)$, then $\rho$ is surjective. Let $A\in\GL(H)$ and $U\in U(H)$. We have \[ \rho(AU) = (AU)(AU)^* = AUU^*A^* = AIA^* = AA^* = \rho(A). \] In particular, we have \begin{align*} \ker(\rho) &= \{A\in\GL(H): \rho(A)=I\} \\ &= \{A\in\GL(H): AA^*=I\} \\ &= U(H). \end{align*} Since $\GL(H)/\ker(\rho)$ is in one-one correspondence with $\rho(\GL(H))=\GL^+(H)$, the quotient space follows.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\rho(A)=AA^*$ is surjective and right-$U(H)$-invariant with kernel $U(H)$, then pass to the quotient.

eq 0}\sup_{x\in X} \|A\|_H  rac{\|f(x)\|_H}{\|f\|_J} \  rac{1}{\|A^{-1}\|_H} \sup_{f\in J,f

nodes.name: Proof of the linear deformation lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\phi\in H$. Then, $A^*\phi\in H$. Since $f$ is a frame, then \[ a\|A^*\phi\|_H^2 \leq \int_X\lvert\langle A^*\phi, f(x)\rangle_H\rvert^2\,d\mu(x) \leq b\|A^*\phi\|_H^2. \] Since $\langle A^*\phi,f(x)\rangle_H = \langle\phi, A[f(x)]\rangle_H = \langle\phi, (Af)(x)\rangle_H$, then \[ a\|A^*\phi\|_H^2 \leq \int_X\lvert\langle \phi, (Af)(x)\rangle_H\rvert^2\,d\mu(x) \leq b\|A^*\phi\|_H^2. \] Since $A\in\GL(H)$ and since $A$ and $A^*$ have the same norms, then we have \[ \frac{a}{\|A^{-1}\|_H^2}\|\phi\|_H^2 = a\left(\frac{\|\phi\|_H}{\|A^{-1}\|_H}\right)^2 \leq a\|A^*\phi\|_H^2. \] We also have \[ b\|A^*\phi\|_H^2 \leq b(\|A\|_H\|\phi\|_H)^2 = b\|A\|_H^2\|\phi\|_H^2. \] Therefore, for all $\phi\in H$, we have \[ \frac{a}{\|A^{-1}\|_H^2}\|\phi\|_H^2 \leq \int_X\lvert\phi,(Af)(x)\rangle_H^2\,d\mu(x) \leq b\|A\|_H^2\|\phi\|_H^2. \] Thus, $Af$ is a frame. The frame operator of $Af$ is given by \begin{align*} S(Af)\phi &= \int_X\langle\phi, (Af)(x)\rangle_H(Af)(x)\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \int_X\langle\phi,A[f(x)]\rangle_HA[f(x)]\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \int_X A\langle A^*\phi, f(x)\rangle_H f(x)\,d\mu(x). \end{align*} Since $A$ is bounded and hence uniformly continuous, then \begin{align*} S(Af)\phi &= A\int_X\langle A^*\phi, f(x)\rangle_H f(x)\,d\mu(x) \\ &= AS(f)A^*\phi. \end{align*} Therefore, $S(Af) = \ad_A(S)$.
nodes.statement_short: Transfer the frame inequality through $A^*$ to get new frame bounds, then pull $A$ out of the frame-operator integral.

nodes.name: Proof of regularity of the action
nodes.statement: The reverse implication is trivial. For the forward implication, suppose $Af=f$. Recall $Af$ is defined by $(Af)(x) = A[f(x)]$ for all $x\in X$. Thus, $Af=f$ implies $A[f(x)] = f(x)$ for all $x\in X$. Since $f$ is a frame on $H$, the set $\{f(x):x\in X\}$ spans $H$. Since $A$ is linear on $H$, we have $A\phi = \phi$ for all $\phi\in H$.
nodes.statement_short: Since the frame elements span $H$, fixing them forces $A$ to be the identity by linearity.

nodes.name: Proof that $S$ is well-defined and surjective
nodes.statement: The frame operator $S(f)$ of a frame $f$ is positive, bounded, and has a bounded inverse. Hence, $S$ is well-defined. Let $B\in\GL^+(H)$. Then, $B=AA^*$ for some $A\in\GL(H)$. Let $f_0\in F_0$ be a Parseval frame, and define $f=Af_0$. By Lemma \ref{LinearDeform}, $f$ is a frame and \[ S(f) = S(Af_0) = \ad_A(S(f_0)) = \ad_A(I) = AA^* = B. \] Ergo, $S$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Well-definedness from positivity of frame operators; surjectivity by deforming a Parseval frame by $A$ with $AA^*=B$.

nodes.name: Proof that $T$ is well-defined and surjective
nodes.statement: Let $f\in F$. By Lemma \ref{LinearDeform}, observe that \[ S(T(f)) = S(S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f) = S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}S(f) S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}} = I. \] Thus, $T(f)\in F_0$, and hence $T$ is well-defined. Note $T$ fixes $F_0$ pointwise: If $f\in F_0$, then $T(f)=I^{-\frac{1}{2}}f=f$. Thus, $T$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $S(T(f))=I$ via the deformation lemma, then note $T$ fixes $F_0$ pointwise.

nodes.name: Proof that Parseval-preserving operators are unitary
nodes.statement: First assume $Af\in F_0$. Then, \[ S(Af) = \ad_A(S(f)) = \ad_A(I) = AA^* = I. \] Hence, $A\in U(H)$. For the converse, suppose $A\in U(H)$. Then, $Af$ is a frame and \[ S(Af) = AA^* = I, \] so that $Af\in F_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Both directions follow from $S(Af)=AA^*$ when $S(f)=I$, so $Af$ Parseval iff $AA^*=I$.

nodes.name: Proof that $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are continuous bijections
nodes.statement: First, we prove $\zeta$ is a bijection: Let $f\in F$. Since $T(f)\in F_0$, then $T(f)$ has the unique factorization $T(f) = U(T(f))\sigma(T(f))$. Note that $S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(T(f))\in \GL(H)$ and $\sigma(T(f))\in \Fbar_0$. We have \begin{align*} \zeta(S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(T(f)), \sigma(T(f))) &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} U(T(f))\sigma(T(f)) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} T(f) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}} f \\ &= f. \end{align*} Thus, $\zeta$ is surjective. Suppose $\zeta(A_1,f_1) = \zeta(A_2,f_2)$. Then, $A_1f_1=A_2f_2$, and hence $(A_2^{-1}A_1)f_1=f_2$. Since $f_1$ and $f_2$ are Parseval, then Lemma \ref{UnitaryParseval} implies that $A_2^{-1}A_1$ is unitary. But since $f_1,f_2\in\Fbar_0$, then either $f_1$ and $f_2$ are unitarily inequivalent or $f_1=f_2$. Since $A_2^{-1}A_1\in U(H)$, then we must have $f_1=f_2$ and hence $A_2^{-1}A_1=I$ By Lemma \ref{Regular}. Thus, $A_1=A_2$. That is, $(A_1,f_1)=(A_2,f_2)$. Ergo, $\zeta$ is injective and therefore bijective. Now, we prove $\zeta^+$ is a bijection: Let $f\in F$. Note $S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}\in\GL^+(H)$ and $T(f)\in F_0$. We have \begin{align*} \zeta^+(S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}, T(f)) &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} T(f) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}} f \\ &= f. \end{align*} Thus, $\zeta^+$ is surjective. Suppose $\zeta^+(A_1,f_1)=\zeta^+(A_2,f_2)$. Thus, $A_1f_1=A_2f_2$, so that $(A_2^{-1}A_1)f_1=f_2$. Since $f_1$ and $f_2$ are Parseval, then Lemma \ref{UnitaryParseval} implies that $A_2^{-1}A_1$ is unitary. Thus, \[ (A_2^{-1}A_1)(A_2^{-1}A_1)^* = A_2^{-1}A_1A_1^*(A_2^{-1})^* = I. \] Since $A_2^{-1}$ and $A_1$ are positive and hence self-adjoint, then \begin{align*} A_2^{-1}A_1A_1A_2^{-1} &= I. \\ A_1^2 &= A_2^2. \end{align*} Since $A_1$ and $A_2$ are positive, then the unique principal square roots of $A_1^2$ and $A_2^2$ are precisely $A_1$ and $A_2$ respectively. Thus, we have $A_1=A_2$. This implies $A_2^{-1}A_1=I$, so that $f_1=f_2$. That is, $(A_1,f_1)=(A_2,f_2)$. Thus, $\zeta^+$ is injective and hence bijective. Finally, we prove $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are both continuous: Since $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are both restrictions of the map $\zeta_*:\GL(H)\times F_0\mapsto F$, then it suffices to show $\zeta_*$ is continuous. Let $\{(A_n,f_n)\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of points in $\GL(H)\times F_0$., and suppose $(A_n,f_n)\rightarrow (A,f)$. This means $A_n\rightarrow A$ and $f_n\rightarrow f$. Let $\eps>0$. Then, there exists $N_1\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N_1$ implies \[ \|A_n-A\|_H,\|f_n-f\|_J <\frac{\eps}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}. \] Since $A_n\rightarrow A$, then there exists $N_2\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N_2$ implies $\|A_n\|_H<2\|A\|_H$. Assume $n>\max\{N_1,N_2\}$. Then, we have \begin{align*} \|\zeta_*(A_n,f_n)-\zeta_*(A,f)\|_J &= \|A_nf_n-Af\|_J \\ &= \|A_nf_n-A_nf+A_nf-Af\|_J \\ &\leq \|A_nf_n-A_nf\|_J+\|A_nf-Af\|_J \\ &= \sup_{x\in X} \|A_n(f_n-f)(x)\|_H+\sup_{x\in X} \|(A_n-A)f(x)\|_H \\ &\leq \|A_n\|_H \sup_{x\in X}\|(f_n-f)(x)\|_H + \|A_n-A\|_H\sup_{x\in X}\|f(x)\|_H \\ &= \|A_n\|_H\|f_n-f\|_J+\|A_n-A\|_H\|f\|_J \\ &< 2\|A\|_H\left(\frac{\eps}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}\right)+\left(\frac{\eps}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}\right)\|f\|_J \\ &= \eps. \end{align*} Ergo, $\zeta_*$ and thus $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity via the factorization $f=S(f)^{1/2}T(f)$, injectivity via unitarity plus regularity (and uniqueness of positive square roots), and continuity by an $\eps$-estimate on the common extension $\zeta_*$.

nodes.name: Proof that $T_1$ is surjective
nodes.statement: Let $f_1\in F_1$. By Corollary \ref{Identity}, we have \begin{align*} f_1 &= \zeta(\pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f_1)), \pi_2(\zeta^{-1}(f_1))) \\ &= \zeta(\pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f_1)), f_{10}) \\ &= \pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f_1)) f_{10} \\ &= T_1(f_1). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the reconstruction identity to any $f_1\in F_1$ and observe the second projection is $f_{10}$, so $f_1=T_1(f_1)$.

nodes.name: Proof that $\theta$ is a bijection
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\GL(H)$. Then, $Af_{10}\in F_1$. By Corollary \ref{Identity}, we have \begin{align*} Af_{10} &= \zeta(\pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(Af_{10})), \pi_2(\zeta^{-1}(Af_{10}))) \\ &= \zeta(\theta(Af_{10})), f_{10}) \\ &= \theta(Af_{10})f_{10}. \end{align*} But since $\GL(H)$ acts regularly on $F_1$ (by Lemma \ref{Regular}), then $\theta(Af_{10})=A$. Ergo, $\theta$ is surjective. Suppose $\theta(f_1) = \theta(f_2)$. As above, $f_1$ and $f_2$ have the unique factorizations $f_1=\theta(f_1)f_{10}$ and $f_2=\theta(f_2)f_{10}$. But since $\theta(f_1)=\theta(f_2)$, then \[ f_1 = \theta(f_1)f_{10} = \theta(f_2)f_{10} = f_2. \] Thus, $\theta$ is injective.
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity from the reconstruction identity plus regularity of the action; injectivity from uniqueness of the factorization $f=\theta(f)f_{10}$.

nodes.name: Proof that $\theta_*$ is a bijection with the stated inverse
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{theta}, $\theta$ is bijective. The identity map is obviously bijective. Thus, the map \[ (f_1,f_0)\rightarrow (\theta(f_1), f_0) \] is a bijection from $F_1\times\Fbar_0$ to $\GL(H)\times\Fbar_0$. By Theorem \ref{zeta}, $\zeta$ is bijective. Ergo, $\theta_*$ is a bijection. To verify that the expression $\theta_*^{-1}$ is indeed the inverse of $\theta_*$, let $f\in F$ and consider \begin{align*} \theta_*(\theta_*^{-1}(f)) &= \zeta(\theta(T_1(f)), \sigma\circ T(f)) \\ &= \zeta[\pi_1\circ\zeta^{-1}(\pi_1\circ\zeta^{-1}(f)f_{10}), \sigma\circ T(f)] \\ &= \zeta(\pi_1\zeta^{-1}(f), \sigma\circ T(f)) \\ &= \pi_1(\zeta(f))\sigma(T(f)) \\ &= f. \end{align*} The reverse composition proceeds similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Compose the bijections $\theta\times\mathrm{id}$ and $\zeta$, then verify $\theta_*\circ\theta_*^{-1}=\mathrm{id}$ by direct substitution.

nodes.name: Proof that continuity of $\zeta^{-1}$ gives a principal fiber bundle
nodes.statement: Suppose $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous. Then, $\theta = \pi_1\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous. By Theorem \ref{zeta}, $\zeta$ is continuous. Thus, $\theta_*(f_1,f_0) = \zeta(\theta(f_1), f_0)$ is continuous Since $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous, then $T_1(f) = \pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f))f_{10}$ and $\sigma\circ T = \pi_1\circ\zeta^{-1}$ are continuous. Thus, $\theta_*^{-1} = (T_1, \sigma\circ T)$ is continuous. Ergo, $\theta_*$ is a homeomorphism. Since $F$ is homeomorphic to the product space $F_1\times\Fbar_0$ (via $\theta_*^{-1}$), then $F$ is trivially a fiber bundle as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of $\zeta^{-1}$ makes both $\theta_*$ and $\theta_*^{-1}$ continuous, so $F\cong F_1\times\Fbar_0$ and the bundle is trivial.

nodes.name: Proof of continuity of $S$ in $J_1$
nodes.statement: Let $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of frames in $F$ and $f\in F$ such that $f_n\rightarrow f$ in $J_1$. Let $\eps>0$. Then, there exists $N\in\NN$ such that $n>N$ implies $\|f_n\|_{J_1}<2\|f\|_{j_1}$ and \[ \|f_n-f\|_{J_1} < \frac{\eps}{3\|f\|_{J_1}}. \] Suppose $n>N$. Consider any $\phi\in H$. We have \begin{align*} \|S(f_n)\phi-S(f)\phi\|_H &= \left\|\int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f_n(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ &= \left\|\int_X \brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f_n(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right. \\ & \qquad + \left.\int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ &= \left\|\int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H [f_n(x)-f(x)]\,d\mu(x) + \int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)-f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ & \leq \int_X \|\phi\|_H\|f_n(x)\|_H\|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H\,d\mu(x)  \\ & \qquad + \int_X\|\phi\|_H\|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H\|f\|_H\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \|\phi\|\int_X \|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H (\|f_n(x)\|_H+\|f(x)\|_H)\,d\mu(x). \end{align*} By H\"{o}lder's Inequality, we have \begin{align*} \|S(f_n)\phi-S(f)\phi\|_H &\leq \|\phi\|_H\int_X\|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H\,d\mu(x)\int_X(\|f_n(x)\|_H+\|f(x)\|_H)\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \|\phi\|_H\|f_n-f\|_{J_1}(\|f_n\|_{J_1}+\|f\|_{J_1}) \\ &< 3\|f\|_{J_1}\|f_n-f\|_{J_1}\|\phi\|_H \\ &< \eps \|\phi\|_H. \end{align*} Since this holds for all $\phi\in H$, then $\|S(f_n)-S(f)\|_H<\eps$. Ergo, $S(f_n)\rightarrow S(f)$, and hence $S$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Sequential continuity via an add-and-subtract splitting of the frame-operator integral followed by H\"{o}lder's inequality.

nodes.name: Proof of continuity of $T$ in $J_1$
nodes.statement: Let $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of frames in $F$ and $f\in F$ such that $f_n\rightarrow f$ in $J_1$. By Lemma \ref{SCont}, $S(f_n)\rightarrow S(f)$. Since the map sending an operator in $\GL(H)$ to its inverse and the map sending an operator in $\GL^+(H)$ to its principal square root are both continuous in the operator norm, then $S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\rightarrow S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. Let $\eps>0$. Then, there exists $N\in\NN$ such that $n>N$ implies $\|f_n\|_{J_1}<2\|f\|_{J_1}$ and \[ \|f-f_n\|_{J_1},\|S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}-S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_H < \delta=\frac{\eps}{2\|f\|_{J_1}+\|S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_H}. \] Suppose $n>N$. We have \begin{align*} \|T(f_n)-T(f)\|_{J_1} &= \|S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f_n-S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f\|_{J_1} \\ &= \|S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f_n-S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f_n+S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f_n-S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f\|_{J_1} \\ &= \|[S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}-S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}]f_n+S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}(f_n-f)\|_{J_1} \\ &\leq \|S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}-S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_H\|f_n\|_{J_1}+\|S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_H\|f_n-f\|_{J_1} \\ &< \delta 2\|f\|_{J_1} + \|S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_H\delta \\ &= \eps. \end{align*} Ergo, $T(f_n)\rightarrow T(f)$, and hence $T$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Combine continuity of $S$ with continuity of inversion and principal square root, then split $T(f_n)-T(f)$ into two controllable terms.

nodes.name: Proof of continuity of $U$ in $J_1$
nodes.statement: Let $f\in F_0$. Then, $f_0$ has the unique factorization $f = U(f)\sigma(f)$. For any $\phi\in H$ and for all $x\in X$, we have \[ \brak{\phi, f(x)}_H = \brak{\phi, U(f)\sigma(f)(x)}_H = \brak{U(f)^*\phi, \sigma(f)(x)}_H. \] Letting $V_g$ and $V_g^*$ denote the analysis and synthesis operators of a frame $g\in F$, we have \[ V_f\phi = V_{\sigma(f)}U(f)^*\phi, \] or simply $V_f = V_{\sigma(f)}U(f)^*$. Thus, $V_fU(f) = V_{\sigma(f)}$, and hence $V_f^*V_fU(f) = V_f^*V_{\sigma(f)}$. But since $f$ is Parseval, then $V_f^*V_f = S(f)=I$ so that \[ U(f) = V_f^* V_{\sigma(f)}. \] Thus, for all $\phi\in H$, we have \begin{equation} U(f)\phi = \int_X\brak{\phi, \sigma(f)(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x). \end{equation} To show $U$ is continuous, let $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of frames in $F_0$ and $f\in F_0$ with $f_n\rightarrow f$ in $J_1$. Since $\sigma$ is continuous, then $\sigma(f_n)\rightarrow\sigma(f)$. Let $\eps>0$. Then, there exists $N\in\NN$ such that $n>N$ implies $\|f_n\|_{J_1}<2\|f\|_{J_1}$ and \[ \|f_n-f\|_{J_1}, \|\sigma(f_n)-\sigma(f)\|_{J_1} < \delta = \frac{\eps}{\|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1}+2\|f\|_{J_1}}. \] Suppose $n>N$. Let $\phi\in H$. By manipulations similar to those used in the proof of Lemma \ref{SCont} (including the Triangle Inequality, Cauchy-Schwartz Inequality, and H\"{o}lder's Inequality), we have \begin{align*} \|U(f_n)\phi-U(f)\phi\|_H &= \left\|\int_X\brak{\phi, \sigma(f_n)(x)}_H f_n(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, \sigma(f)(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ &\leq \|\phi\|_H \|\sigma(f_n)-\sigma(f)\|_{J_1}\|f_n\|_{J_1} + \|\phi\|_H \|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1} \|f_n-f\|_{J_1} \\ &< \|\phi\|_H \delta 2\|f\|_{J_1} + \|\phi\|_H \|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1} \delta \\ &= (2\|f\|_{J_1}+\|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1})\delta \|\phi\|_H \\ &= \eps \|\phi\|_H. \end{align*} Since this holds for all $\phi\in H$, then $\|U(f_n)-U(f)\|_H < \eps$. Ergo, $U(f_n)\rightarrow U(f)$, and hence $U$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Derive the integral formula $U(f)=V_f^*V_{\sigma(f)}$ from the Parseval condition, then repeat the H\"{o}lder estimate of Lemma SCont.

nodes.name: Proof that $F$ is a principal fiber bundle in $J_1$
nodes.statement: Recall that $\zeta^{-1}$ is given by \[ \zeta^{-1}(f) = (S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(f), \sigma\circ T(f)). \] By Lemmas \ref{SCont}-\ref{UCont}, the maps $S$, $T$, and $U$ are continuous in $J_1$. Moreover, $\sigma$ and the square root function are continuous as well. Therefore, $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous. By Proposition \ref{IfzetaCont}, $F$ is a fiber bundle as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Assemble continuity of $S$, $T$, $U$, $\sigma$ and the square root to get $\zeta^{-1}$ continuous, then invoke the sufficient condition.

nodes.name: Reflexivity
nodes.statement: Let $B\in\GL(H)$. Clearly, $\ad_I(B)=IBI^*=B$, so that $B\sim B$. Thus, $\sim$ is reflexive.
nodes.statement_short: Take $A=I$ to get $B\sim B$.

nodes.name: Symmetry
nodes.statement: Given $B,B^\prime\in\GL(H)$, suppose $B\sim B^\prime$. That is, $ad_A(B)=ABA*=B^\prime$ for some $A\in\GL(H)$. Then, \[ \ad_{A^{-1}}(B^\prime) = A^{-1}B^\prime (A^{-1})^* = A^{-1}ABA^*(A^*)^{-1} = B. \] Thus, $B^\prime\sim B$, and hence $\sim$ is symmetric.
nodes.statement_short: Adjugate by $A^{-1}$ to reverse the relation.

nodes.name: Transitivity
nodes.statement: Finally, suppose $B\sim B^\prime$ and $B^\prime\sim B^{\prime\prime}$. Thus, $\ad_A(B)=ABA^*=B^\prime$ and $\ad_{A^\prime}(B^\prime)=A^\prime B^\prime (A^\prime)^*=B^{\prime\prime}$ for some $A,A^\prime\in\GL(H)$. Then, \[ \ad_{A^\prime A}(B) = A^\prime AB(A^\prime A)^* = A^\prime (ABA^*)(A^\prime)^* = A^\prime B^\prime (A^\prime)^* = B^{\prime\prime}. \] Thus, $B\sim B^{\prime\prime}$, and hence $\sim$ is transitive.
nodes.statement_short: Compose adjugations via $A^\prime A$.

nodes.name: Positivity is closed under adjugation
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\GL(H)$ and $B\in\GL^+(H)$. For any $\phi\in H$, we have \[ \brak{\ad_A(B)\phi, \phi} = \brak{ABA^*\phi, \phi} = \brak{BA^*\phi, A^*\phi}\geq 0, \] where the inequality holds since $A^*\phi\in H$ and $B$ is positive. Thus, $\ad_A(B)$ is positive, so that $GL^+(H)$ is closed under adjugation.
nodes.statement_short: Move $A^*$ across the inner product to see $\ad_A(B)$ is positive.

nodes.name: Any two positive operators are adjugate
nodes.statement: Let $B,C\in\GL^+(H)$. Since $B,C$ are positive, then $B=SS^*$ and $C=TT^*$ for some $S,T\in\GL(H)$. There exists $A\in\GL(H)$ such that $T=AS$. We have \[ \ad_A(B) = ABA^* = ASS^*A^* = (AS)(AS)^* = TT^* = C. \] Thus, $B\sim C$. Ergo, $\GL^+(H)$ is an adjugacy class.
nodes.statement_short: Use factorizations $B=SS^*$, $C=TT^*$ and $A=TS^{-1}$ to conclude $B\sim C$.

nodes.name: $\rho$ is surjective
nodes.statement: Since every positive operator $B\in\GL^+(H)$ can be written in the form $B=AA^*$ with $A\in\GL(H)$, then $\rho$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Surjectivity from the factorization $B=AA^*$.

nodes.name: Invariance under right unitary multiplication
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\GL(H)$ and $U\in U(H)$. We have \[ \rho(AU) = (AU)(AU)^* = AUU^*A^* = AIA^* = AA^* = \rho(A). \]
nodes.statement_short: Show $\rho(AU)=\rho(A)$ for unitary $U$.

nodes.name: Kernel computation and quotient
nodes.statement: In particular, we have \begin{align*} \ker(\rho) &= \{A\in\GL(H): \rho(A)=I\} \\ &= \{A\in\GL(H): AA^*=I\} \\ &= U(H). \end{align*} Since $\GL(H)/\ker(\rho)$ is in one-one correspondence with $\rho(\GL(H))=\GL^+(H)$, the quotient space follows.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\ker(\rho)=U(H)$ and pass to the quotient.

nodes.name: Express the operator norm on $J$
nodes.statement: We have the operator norm \[ \|A\|_J = \sup_{f\in J,f\neq 0} \frac{\|Af\|_J}{\|f\|_J} = \sup_{f\in J,f\neq 0}\sup_{x\in X} \frac{\|Af(x)\|_H}{\|f\|_J}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Write $\|A\|_J$ as a double supremum over $f$ and $x$.

nodes.name: Two-sided bound on $\|A\|_J$
nodes.statement:
Since $A\in\GL(H)$, then we have  egin{align*} \sup_{f\in J,f
eq 0}\sup_{x\in X}  rac{1}{\|A^{-1}\|_H} rac{\|f(x)\|_H}{\|f\|_J} \leq &\|A\|_J \leq \sup_{f\in J,f
eq 0}\sup_{x\in X} \|A\|_H  rac{\|f(x)\|_H}{\|f\|_J} \  rac{1}{\|A^{-1}\|_H} \sup_{f\in J,f
eq 0}\sup_{x\in X} rac{\|f(x)\|_H}{\|f\|_J} \leq &\|A\|_J \leq \|A\|_H\sup_{f\in J,f
eq 0}\sup_{x\in X} rac{\|f(x)\|_H}{\|f\|_J} \  rac{1}{\|A^{-1}\|_H}\sup_{f\in J,f
eq 0}  rac{\|f\|_J}{\|f\|_J} \leq &\|A\|_J \leq \|A\|_H\sup_{f\in J,f
eq 0}  rac{\|f\|_J}{\|f\|_J} \  rac{1}{\|A^{-1}\|_H} \leq &\|A\|_J \leq \|A\|_H. \end{align*} Therefore, $A\in\GL(J)$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the suprema above and below by the $H$-operator norms of $A$ and $A^{-1}$.

nodes.name: $Af$ is a frame
nodes.statement: Let $\phi\in H$. Then, $A^*\phi\in H$. Since $f$ is a frame, then \[ a\|A^*\phi\|_H^2 \leq \int_X\lvert\langle A^*\phi, f(x)\rangle_H\rvert^2\,d\mu(x) \leq b\|A^*\phi\|_H^2. \] Since $\langle A^*\phi,f(x)\rangle_H = \langle\phi, A[f(x)]\rangle_H = \langle\phi, (Af)(x)\rangle_H$, then \[ a\|A^*\phi\|_H^2 \leq \int_X\lvert\langle \phi, (Af)(x)\rangle_H\rvert^2\,d\mu(x) \leq b\|A^*\phi\|_H^2. \] Since $A\in\GL(H)$ and since $A$ and $A^*$ have the same norms, then we have \[ \frac{a}{\|A^{-1}\|_H^2}\|\phi\|_H^2 = a\left(\frac{\|\phi\|_H}{\|A^{-1}\|_H}\right)^2 \leq a\|A^*\phi\|_H^2. \] We also have \[ b\|A^*\phi\|_H^2 \leq b(\|A\|_H\|\phi\|_H)^2 = b\|A\|_H^2\|\phi\|_H^2. \] Therefore, for all $\phi\in H$, we have \[ \frac{a}{\|A^{-1}\|_H^2}\|\phi\|_H^2 \leq \int_X\lvert\phi,(Af)(x)\rangle_H^2\,d\mu(x) \leq b\|A\|_H^2\|\phi\|_H^2. \] Thus, $Af$ is a frame.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the frame inequality at $A^*\phi$ and re-bound both sides in terms of $\|\phi\|$.

nodes.name: Compute the frame operator of $Af$
nodes.statement: The frame operator of $Af$ is given by \begin{align*} S(Af)\phi &= \int_X\langle\phi, (Af)(x)\rangle_H(Af)(x)\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \int_X\langle\phi,A[f(x)]\rangle_HA[f(x)]\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \int_X A\langle A^*\phi, f(x)\rangle_H f(x)\,d\mu(x). \end{align*} Since $A$ is bounded and hence uniformly continuous, then \begin{align*} S(Af)\phi &= A\int_X\langle A^*\phi, f(x)\rangle_H f(x)\,d\mu(x) \\ &= AS(f)A^*\phi. \end{align*} Therefore, $S(Af) = \ad_A(S)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pull $A$ out of the integral using boundedness to get $S(Af)=AS(f)A^*$.

nodes.name: Reverse implication
nodes.statement: The reverse implication is trivial.
nodes.statement_short: $A=I$ clearly fixes $f$.

nodes.name: Forward implication via spanning
nodes.statement: For the forward implication, suppose $Af=f$. Recall $Af$ is defined by $(Af)(x) = A[f(x)]$ for all $x\in X$. Thus, $Af=f$ implies $A[f(x)] = f(x)$ for all $x\in X$. Since $f$ is a frame on $H$, the set $\{f(x):x\in X\}$ spans $H$. Since $A$ is linear on $H$, we have $A\phi = \phi$ for all $\phi\in H$.
nodes.statement_short: Frame elements span $H$, so fixing them and linearity give $A=I$.

nodes.name: $S$ is well-defined
nodes.statement: The frame operator $S(f)$ of a frame $f$ is positive, bounded, and has a bounded inverse. Hence, $S$ is well-defined.
nodes.statement_short: Well-definedness from the properties of frame operators.

nodes.name: $S$ is surjective
nodes.statement: Let $B\in\GL^+(H)$. Then, $B=AA^*$ for some $A\in\GL(H)$. Let $f_0\in F_0$ be a Parseval frame, and define $f=Af_0$. By Lemma \ref{LinearDeform}, $f$ is a frame and \[ S(f) = S(Af_0) = \ad_A(S(f_0)) = \ad_A(I) = AA^* = B. \] Ergo, $S$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Deform a Parseval frame by $A$ with $AA^*=B$ to hit an arbitrary positive $B$.

nodes.name: $T$ is well-defined
nodes.statement: Let $f\in F$. By Lemma \ref{LinearDeform}, observe that \[ S(T(f)) = S(S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}f) = S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}S(f) S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}} = I. \] Thus, $T(f)\in F_0$, and hence $T$ is well-defined.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $S(T(f))=I$ using the deformation lemma.

nodes.name: $T$ fixes $F_0$ and is surjective
nodes.statement: Note $T$ fixes $F_0$ pointwise: If $f\in F_0$, then $T(f)=I^{-\frac{1}{2}}f=f$. Thus, $T$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: $T$ restricted to $F_0$ is the identity, hence surjective.

nodes.name: Forward direction: $Af$ Parseval implies $A$ unitary
nodes.statement: First assume $Af\in F_0$. Then, \[ S(Af) = \ad_A(S(f)) = \ad_A(I) = AA^* = I. \] Hence, $A\in U(H)$.
nodes.statement_short: $S(Af)=AA^*=I$ forces $A$ unitary.

nodes.name: Converse: unitary $A$ preserves Parseval
nodes.statement: For the converse, suppose $A\in U(H)$. Then, $Af$ is a frame and \[ S(Af) = AA^* = I, \] so that $Af\in F_0$.
nodes.statement_short: For unitary $A$, $S(Af)=I$ so $Af$ is Parseval.

nodes.name: $\zeta$ is surjective
nodes.statement: First, we prove $\zeta$ is a bijection: Let $f\in F$. Since $T(f)\in F_0$, then $T(f)$ has the unique factorization $T(f) = U(T(f))\sigma(T(f))$. Note that $S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(T(f))\in \GL(H)$ and $\sigma(T(f))\in \Fbar_0$. We have \begin{align*} \zeta(S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(T(f)), \sigma(T(f))) &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} U(T(f))\sigma(T(f)) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} T(f) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}} f \\ &= f. \end{align*} Thus, $\zeta$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit a preimage of $f$ using the factorization $f=S(f)^{1/2}U(T(f))\sigma(T(f))$.

nodes.name: $\zeta$ is injective
nodes.statement: Suppose $\zeta(A_1,f_1) = \zeta(A_2,f_2)$. Then, $A_1f_1=A_2f_2$, and hence $(A_2^{-1}A_1)f_1=f_2$. Since $f_1$ and $f_2$ are Parseval, then Lemma \ref{UnitaryParseval} implies that $A_2^{-1}A_1$ is unitary. But since $f_1,f_2\in\Fbar_0$, then either $f_1$ and $f_2$ are unitarily inequivalent or $f_1=f_2$. Since $A_2^{-1}A_1\in U(H)$, then we must have $f_1=f_2$ and hence $A_2^{-1}A_1=I$ By Lemma \ref{Regular}. Thus, $A_1=A_2$. That is, $(A_1,f_1)=(A_2,f_2)$. Ergo, $\zeta$ is injective and therefore bijective.
nodes.statement_short: Unitarity of $A_2^{-1}A_1$ plus inequivalence in $\Fbar_0$ and regularity force $(A_1,f_1)=(A_2,f_2)$.

nodes.name: $\zeta^+$ is surjective
nodes.statement: Now, we prove $\zeta^+$ is a bijection: Let $f\in F$. Note $S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}\in\GL^+(H)$ and $T(f)\in F_0$. We have \begin{align*} \zeta^+(S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}, T(f)) &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} T(f) \\ &= S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}} S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}} f \\ &= f. \end{align*} Thus, $\zeta^+$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: The pair $(S(f)^{1/2},T(f))$ maps to $f$ under $\zeta^+$.

nodes.name: $\zeta^+$ is injective
nodes.statement: Suppose $\zeta^+(A_1,f_1)=\zeta^+(A_2,f_2)$. Thus, $A_1f_1=A_2f_2$, so that $(A_2^{-1}A_1)f_1=f_2$. Since $f_1$ and $f_2$ are Parseval, then Lemma \ref{UnitaryParseval} implies that $A_2^{-1}A_1$ is unitary. Thus, \[ (A_2^{-1}A_1)(A_2^{-1}A_1)^* = A_2^{-1}A_1A_1^*(A_2^{-1})^* = I. \] Since $A_2^{-1}$ and $A_1$ are positive and hence self-adjoint, then \begin{align*} A_2^{-1}A_1A_1A_2^{-1} &= I. \\ A_1^2 &= A_2^2. \end{align*} Since $A_1$ and $A_2$ are positive, then the unique principal square roots of $A_1^2$ and $A_2^2$ are precisely $A_1$ and $A_2$ respectively. Thus, we have $A_1=A_2$. This implies $A_2^{-1}A_1=I$, so that $f_1=f_2$. That is, $(A_1,f_1)=(A_2,f_2)$. Thus, $\zeta^+$ is injective and hence bijective.
nodes.statement_short: Self-adjointness gives $A_1^2=A_2^2$, and uniqueness of positive square roots gives $A_1=A_2$.

nodes.name: Continuity of $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ via $\zeta_*$
nodes.statement: Finally, we prove $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are both continuous: Since $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are both restrictions of the map $\zeta_*:\GL(H)\times F_0\mapsto F$, then it suffices to show $\zeta_*$ is continuous. Let $\{(A_n,f_n)\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of points in $\GL(H)\times F_0$., and suppose $(A_n,f_n)\rightarrow (A,f)$. This means $A_n\rightarrow A$ and $f_n\rightarrow f$. Let $\eps>0$. Then, there exists $N_1\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N_1$ implies \[ \|A_n-A\|_H,\|f_n-f\|_J <\frac{\eps}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}. \] Since $A_n\rightarrow A$, then there exists $N_2\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $n>N_2$ implies $\|A_n\|_H<2\|A\|_H$. Assume $n>\max\{N_1,N_2\}$. Then, we have \begin{align*} \|\zeta_*(A_n,f_n)-\zeta_*(A,f)\|_J &= \|A_nf_n-Af\|_J \\ &= \|A_nf_n-A_nf+A_nf-Af\|_J \\ &\leq \|A_nf_n-A_nf\|_J+\|A_nf-Af\|_J \\ &= \sup_{x\in X} \|A_n(f_n-f)(x)\|_H+\sup_{x\in X} \|(A_n-A)f(x)\|_H \\ &\leq \|A_n\|_H \sup_{x\in X}\|(f_n-f)(x)\|_H + \|A_n-A\|_H\sup_{x\in X}\|f(x)\|_H \\ &= \|A_n\|_H\|f_n-f\|_J+\|A_n-A\|_H\|f\|_J \\ &< 2\|A\|_H\left(\frac{\eps}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}\right)+\left(\frac{\eps}{2\|A\|_H+\|f\|_J}\right)\|f\|_J \\ &= \eps. \end{align*} Ergo, $\zeta_*$ and thus $\zeta$ and $\zeta^+$ are continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Add-and-subtract estimate on the common extension $\zeta_*$ gives sequential continuity.

nodes.name: $\theta$ is surjective
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\GL(H)$. Then, $Af_{10}\in F_1$. By Corollary \ref{Identity}, we have \begin{align*} Af_{10} &= \zeta(\pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(Af_{10})), \pi_2(\zeta^{-1}(Af_{10}))) \\ &= \zeta(\theta(Af_{10})), f_{10}) \\ &= \theta(Af_{10})f_{10}. \end{align*} But since $\GL(H)$ acts regularly on $F_1$ (by Lemma \ref{Regular}), then $\theta(Af_{10})=A$. Ergo, $\theta$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the reconstruction identity to $Af_{10}$ and use regularity to get $\theta(Af_{10})=A$.

nodes.name: $\theta$ is injective
nodes.statement: Suppose $\theta(f_1) = \theta(f_2)$. As above, $f_1$ and $f_2$ have the unique factorizations $f_1=\theta(f_1)f_{10}$ and $f_2=\theta(f_2)f_{10}$. But since $\theta(f_1)=\theta(f_2)$, then \[ f_1 = \theta(f_1)f_{10} = \theta(f_2)f_{10} = f_2. \] Thus, $\theta$ is injective.
nodes.statement_short: Equal $\theta$-values give equal factorizations, hence $f_1=f_2$.

nodes.name: $\theta_*$ is a bijection
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{theta}, $\theta$ is bijective. The identity map is obviously bijective. Thus, the map \[ (f_1,f_0)\rightarrow (\theta(f_1), f_0) \] is a bijection from $F_1\times\Fbar_0$ to $\GL(H)\times\Fbar_0$. By Theorem \ref{zeta}, $\zeta$ is bijective. Ergo, $\theta_*$ is a bijection.
nodes.statement_short: Compose the bijection $\theta\times\mathrm{id}$ with the bijection $\zeta$.

nodes.name: Verify the stated inverse
nodes.statement: To verify that the expression $\theta_*^{-1}$ is indeed the inverse of $\theta_*$, let $f\in F$ and consider \begin{align*} \theta_*(\theta_*^{-1}(f)) &= \zeta(\theta(T_1(f)), \sigma\circ T(f)) \\ &= \zeta[\pi_1\circ\zeta^{-1}(\pi_1\circ\zeta^{-1}(f)f_{10}), \sigma\circ T(f)] \\ &= \zeta(\pi_1\zeta^{-1}(f), \sigma\circ T(f)) \\ &= \pi_1(\zeta(f))\sigma(T(f)) \\ &= f. \end{align*} The reverse composition proceeds similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Direct substitution shows $\theta_*\circ\theta_*^{-1}=\mathrm{id}$.

nodes.name: $\theta_*$ is continuous
nodes.statement: Suppose $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous. Then, $\theta = \pi_1\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous. By Theorem \ref{zeta}, $\zeta$ is continuous. Thus, $\theta_*(f_1,f_0) = \zeta(\theta(f_1), f_0)$ is continuous
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of $\zeta^{-1}$ and $\zeta$ makes the composite $\theta_*$ continuous.

nodes.name: $\theta_*^{-1}$ is continuous
nodes.statement: Since $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous, then $T_1(f) = \pi_1(\zeta^{-1}(f))f_{10}$ and $\sigma\circ T = \pi_1\circ\zeta^{-1}$ are continuous. Thus, $\theta_*^{-1} = (T_1, \sigma\circ T)$ is continuous. Ergo, $\theta_*$ is a homeomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Both components of $\theta_*^{-1}$ are continuous, so $\theta_*$ is a homeomorphism.

nodes.name: Conclude the bundle structure
nodes.statement: Since $F$ is homeomorphic to the product space $F_1\times\Fbar_0$ (via $\theta_*^{-1}$), then $F$ is trivially a fiber bundle as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: A global product structure makes $F$ a (trivial) fiber bundle.

nodes.name: Choose $N$ for the $J_1$-convergent sequence
nodes.statement: Let $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of frames in $F$ and $f\in F$ such that $f_n\rightarrow f$ in $J_1$. Let $\eps>0$. Then, there exists $N\in\NN$ such that $n>N$ implies $\|f_n\|_{J_1}<2\|f\|_{j_1}$ and \[ \|f_n-f\|_{J_1} < \frac{\eps}{3\|f\|_{J_1}}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Set up the convergent sequence and pick $N$ controlling $\|f_n-f\|_{J_1}$.

nodes.name: Split the frame-operator difference
nodes.statement: Suppose $n>N$. Consider any $\phi\in H$. We have \begin{align*} \|S(f_n)\phi-S(f)\phi\|_H &= \left\|\int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f_n(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ &= \left\|\int_X \brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f_n(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right. \\ & \qquad + \left.\int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ &= \left\|\int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)}_H [f_n(x)-f(x)]\,d\mu(x) + \int_X\brak{\phi, f_n(x)-f(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ & \leq \int_X \|\phi\|_H\|f_n(x)\|_H\|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H\,d\mu(x)  \\ & \qquad + \int_X\|\phi\|_H\|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H\|f\|_H\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \|\phi\|\int_X \|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H (\|f_n(x)\|_H+\|f(x)\|_H)\,d\mu(x). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Add and subtract a cross term, then apply Cauchy-Schwarz pointwise.

nodes.name: Apply H\"{o}lder's Inequality and conclude
nodes.statement: By H\"{o}lder's Inequality, we have \begin{align*} \|S(f_n)\phi-S(f)\phi\|_H &\leq \|\phi\|_H\int_X\|f_n(x)-f(x)\|_H\,d\mu(x)\int_X(\|f_n(x)\|_H+\|f(x)\|_H)\,d\mu(x) \\ &= \|\phi\|_H\|f_n-f\|_{J_1}(\|f_n\|_{J_1}+\|f\|_{J_1}) \\ &< 3\|f\|_{J_1}\|f_n-f\|_{J_1}\|\phi\|_H \\ &< \eps \|\phi\|_H. \end{align*} Since this holds for all $\phi\in H$, then $\|S(f_n)-S(f)\|_H<\eps$. Ergo, $S(f_n)\rightarrow S(f)$, and hence $S$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: H\"{o}lder's inequality converts the integral bound into $J_1$ norms, giving $\eps$-continuity.

nodes.name: Continuity of inversion and square root
nodes.statement: Let $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of frames in $F$ and $f\in F$ such that $f_n\rightarrow f$ in $J_1$. By Lemma \ref{SCont}, $S(f_n)\rightarrow S(f)$. Since the map sending an operator in $\GL(H)$ to its inverse and the map sending an operator in $\GL^+(H)$ to its principal square root are both continuous in the operator norm, then $S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\rightarrow S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. Let $\eps>0$. Then, there exists $N\in\NN$ such that $n>N$ implies $\|f_n\|_{J_1}<2\|f\|_{J_1}$ and \[ \|f-f_n\|_{J_1},\|S(f_n)^{-\frac{1}{2}}-S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_H < \delta=\frac{\eps}{2\|f\|_{J_1}+\|S(f)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_H}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Use continuity of $S$, inversion, and principal square root to get $S(f_n)^{-1/2}\to S(f)^{-1/2}$, then choose $\delta$.

nodes.name: Estimate $\|T(f_n)-T(f)\|_{J_1}$
nodes.statement_short: Add-and-subtract split plus the triangle inequality bounds the difference by $\eps$.

nodes.name: Integral formula $U(f)=V_f^*V_{\sigma(f)}$
nodes.statement: Let $f\in F_0$. Then, $f_0$ has the unique factorization $f = U(f)\sigma(f)$. For any $\phi\in H$ and for all $x\in X$, we have \[ \brak{\phi, f(x)}_H = \brak{\phi, U(f)\sigma(f)(x)}_H = \brak{U(f)^*\phi, \sigma(f)(x)}_H. \] Letting $V_g$ and $V_g^*$ denote the analysis and synthesis operators of a frame $g\in F$, we have \[ V_f\phi = V_{\sigma(f)}U(f)^*\phi, \] or simply $V_f = V_{\sigma(f)}U(f)^*$. Thus, $V_fU(f) = V_{\sigma(f)}$, and hence $V_f^*V_fU(f) = V_f^*V_{\sigma(f)}$. But since $f$ is Parseval, then $V_f^*V_f = S(f)=I$ so that \[ U(f) = V_f^* V_{\sigma(f)}. \] Thus, for all $\phi\in H$, we have \begin{equation} U(f)\phi = \int_X\brak{\phi, \sigma(f)(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Derive an explicit integral representation of $U(f)$ from the factorization and the Parseval identity $V_f^*V_f=I$.

nodes.name: Continuity estimate for $U$
nodes.statement: To show $U$ is continuous, let $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of frames in $F_0$ and $f\in F_0$ with $f_n\rightarrow f$ in $J_1$. Since $\sigma$ is continuous, then $\sigma(f_n)\rightarrow\sigma(f)$. Let $\eps>0$. Then, there exists $N\in\NN$ such that $n>N$ implies $\|f_n\|_{J_1}<2\|f\|_{J_1}$ and \[ \|f_n-f\|_{J_1}, \|\sigma(f_n)-\sigma(f)\|_{J_1} < \delta = \frac{\eps}{\|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1}+2\|f\|_{J_1}}. \] Suppose $n>N$. Let $\phi\in H$. By manipulations similar to those used in the proof of Lemma \ref{SCont} (including the Triangle Inequality, Cauchy-Schwartz Inequality, and H\"{o}lder's Inequality), we have \begin{align*} \|U(f_n)\phi-U(f)\phi\|_H &= \left\|\int_X\brak{\phi, \sigma(f_n)(x)}_H f_n(x)\,d\mu(x) - \int_X\brak{\phi, \sigma(f)(x)}_H f(x)\,d\mu(x)\right\| \\ &\leq \|\phi\|_H \|\sigma(f_n)-\sigma(f)\|_{J_1}\|f_n\|_{J_1} + \|\phi\|_H \|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1} \|f_n-f\|_{J_1} \\ &< \|\phi\|_H \delta 2\|f\|_{J_1} + \|\phi\|_H \|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1} \delta \\ &= (2\|f\|_{J_1}+\|\sigma(f)\|_{J_1})\delta \|\phi\|_H \\ &= \eps \|\phi\|_H. \end{align*} Since this holds for all $\phi\in H$, then $\|U(f_n)-U(f)\|_H < \eps$. Ergo, $U(f_n)\rightarrow U(f)$, and hence $U$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the Lemma-SCont estimate on the integral formula, using continuity of $\sigma$.

nodes.name: Continuity of $\zeta^{-1}$ from its components
nodes.statement: Recall that $\zeta^{-1}$ is given by \[ \zeta^{-1}(f) = (S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(f), \sigma\circ T(f)). \] By Lemmas \ref{SCont}-\ref{UCont}, the maps $S$, $T$, and $U$ are continuous in $J_1$. Moreover, $\sigma$ and the square root function are continuous as well. Therefore, $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Each factor of $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous, hence so is $\zeta^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Invoke the sufficient condition
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{IfzetaCont}, $F$ is a fiber bundle as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the sufficient condition to conclude the bundle structure.

nodes.name: Standing hypotheses on $H$, $X$, and $\mu$
nodes.statement: For the remainder of the paper, let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with the inner product $\brak{\cdot,\cdot}$ linear in the first argument. Let the indexing set $X$ be a locally compact space with positive Borel measure $\mu.$

nodes.name: All frames are integrable ($F\subset J_1$)
nodes.statement: Suppose that $F\subset J_1$. That is, suppose that all frames (in $J$) on $H$ are integrable.

nodes.name: $\Fbar_0$ is a continuous transversal
nodes.statement: Suppose $\Fbar_0$ is a continuous transversal of $F/\GL(H)$. That is, suppose that the projection $\sigma:F_0\mapsto\Fbar_0$ is continuous in the topology of $J_1$.

nodes.name: Separable $H$ and measure space $(X,\mu)$
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a separable Hilbert space and let $\left( X,\mu \right) $ be a measure space where the cardinality of $X$ is at least the dimension of $H.$

nodes.name: Is $\zeta^{-1}$ continuous?
nodes.statement: But we cannot conclude this immediately because we do not know whether $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Whether $\zeta^{-1}$ is continuous (and hence $F$ a principal bundle) is not known in general.

nodes.name: Explicit form of $\zeta^{-1}$
nodes.statement: By the commuting diagram in Section 2 and the unique factorization granted by Corollary \ref{Factorization}, it is straightforward to show that $\zeta^{-1}:F\mapsto\GL(H)\times\Fbar_0$ is given by \begin{equation} \zeta^{-1}(f) = (S(f)^{\frac{1}{2}}U(f), \sigma\circ T(f)). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\zeta^{-1}$ sends a frame to the pair (positive-times-unitary operator, transversal Parseval frame).

nodes.name: Two Parseval frames that are not unitarily equivalent
nodes.statement: For example, let $X=[0,d)$ under Lesbesgue measure, where $d$ is the dimension of $H$ and may be infinite, and let $\left\{ h_{k}\right\} _{k=0}^{d-1}$ be an orthonormal basis for $H.$ Then the $H$ valued function $$ F\left( x\right) =e^{i2\pi x}\ h_{_{\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor }}, $$ where $\left\lfloor \; \right\rfloor $ is the floor function, is a frame on $H$.  Any unitary operator $U$ such that $$ U\left[ F\left( x\right) \right] = h_{\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor } $$ would necessarily imply $U\left[ F\left( k\right) \right] =h_{k},$ thus implying that $U=I.$ However, $$U\left[ F\left( k+\frac{1}{2}\right) \right] =-h_{k}$$ implies that $U\neq I,$ and consequently, $F\left( x\right) $ is not unitarily equivalent to $\left\{ h_{k}\right\} .$
nodes.statement_short: The phase-modulated frame $e^{i2\pi x}h_{\lfloor x\rfloor}$ is Parseval but not unitarily equivalent to the orthonormal basis $\{h_k\}$.

nodes.name: A Parseval frame built from two orthonormal bases
nodes.statement: For example, if both $\left\{ f_{k}\right\} _{k=0}^{d-1}$ and $\left\{ h_{k}\right\} _{k=0}^{d-1}$ are orthonormal bases of $H,$ and if we define $$ F\left( x\right) =\cos \left( 2\pi x\right) f_{\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor}+i\sin \left( 2\pi x\right) h_{\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor }, $$ then for any $\phi \in H,$ we notice that $$ \int_{0}^{d}\left\vert \left\langle \phi ,F\left( x\right) \right\rangle \right\vert ^{2}dx=\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\int_{k}^{k+1}\left\vert \left\langle \phi ,F\left( x\right) \right\rangle \right\vert ^{2}dx=\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\int_{0}^{1}\left\vert \left\langle \phi ,F\left( \xi +k\right) \right\rangle \right\vert ^{2}d\xi $$ and $F\left( \xi +k\right) =\cos \left( 2\pi \xi \right) f_{k}+i\sin \left(2\pi \xi \right) h_{k},$ from which it follows that $F\left( x\right) $ is also a Parseval frame.
nodes.statement_short: Interpolating two orthonormal bases by $\cos$/$i\sin$ over $[0,d)$ yields a Parseval frame.

nodes.name: Product-space Parseval frame $K(x,y)$
nodes.statement: Moreover, if $F\left( x\right) $ and $G\left(x\right) $ are both Parseval frames over $H,$ then define $$ K\left( x,y\right) = \cos \left( 2\pi y\right) F\left( x\right) +i\sin \left( 2\pi y\right) G\left( x\right) $$ for $y$ in $[0,1].$ The same approach as above shows that $K\left(x,y\right)$ over $X\times Y$ is also a Parseval frame, and in fact, the same approach leads to the following proposition:
nodes.statement_short: Combining two Parseval frames with $\cos$/$i\sin$ weights gives a Parseval frame over the product index space.

nodes.name: M\"{o}bius strip as a fiber bundle
nodes.statement: A less trivial example of a fiber bundle is the M\"{o}bius strip with base space the circle $S^1$ and fiber $[0, 1]$. For more information on fiber bundles, see \cite{steenrod1951topology}.

nodes.name: Finite frames in $\mathbb{C}^m$ via the singular value decomposition
nodes.statement: For an $m$-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ and a finite index set $X=\left\{ 1,\ldots ,n\right\} ,$ where $m\leq n,$ both of these concepts are well understood. Given $\left\{ f_{1},\ldots ,f_{n}\right\} \subset \mathbb{C}^{m},$ we form the matrix $$ T=\left[  \begin{array}{c} f_{1}^{\ast } \\ \vdots        \\ f_{n}^{\ast } \end{array} \right] $$ where $f_{j}^{\ast }$ is the Hermitian transpose of the column vector $f_{j}.$ The singular value decomposition of $T$ is given by $$ T=U\tilde{\Sigma}V^{\ast }\ \ where\ \ \tilde{\Sigma}= \left[  \begin{array}{c} \Sigma  \\ 0 \end{array} \right] $$ with $\Sigma =diag\left( s_{1},\ldots ,s_{m}\right);$ where $s_{1}\geq \ldots \geq s_{m}\geq 0$ are the singular values of $T;$ where $U:\mathbb{C}^{n}\mapsto \mathbb{C}^{n}$ is unitary; and where $V:\mathbb{C}^{m}\mapsto \mathbb{C}^{m}$ is also unitary. \ For any $\phi \in \mathbb{C}^{m},$ it follows that $$ \left\Vert T\phi \right\Vert ^{2}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left\vert \left\langle \phi, f_{k}\right\rangle \right\vert ^{2} $$ and from the properties of the singular value decomposition, $$s_{m}^{2}\left\Vert \phi \right\Vert ^{2}\leq \left\Vert T\phi \right\Vert^{2}\leq s_{1}^{2}\ \left\Vert \phi \right\Vert ^{2}$$
nodes.statement_short: The finite-dimensional case: stacking $f_j^*$ into $T$ and reading frame bounds off the singular values of $T$.

nodes.name: Singular value decomposition of a frame matrix
nodes.statement: A frame matrix has a singular value decomposition of \[ T=U\tilde{\Sigma}V^{\ast }\ \ where\ \ \tilde{\Sigma}= \left[ \begin{array}{c} \Sigma  \\ 0 \end{array} \right] \]
nodes.statement_short: A frame matrix factors as $U\tilde{\Sigma}V^*$ with $\tilde{\Sigma}$ the padded singular value matrix.

nodes.name: Frame elements need not be independent or distinct
nodes.statement: Note that the range of $f(X)$ need not be a linearly independent set even if $X$ is countable. Note also that $f:X\mapsto H$ is not required to be injective.

nodes.name: Interpretation of the analysis operator
nodes.statement: The analysis operator maps a vector in $H$ to a function in $L^2(X)$ describing the projections of the vector on the frame elements.

nodes.name: Duality is symmetric and non-unique
nodes.statement: If $S$ is the frame operator of $f$, then $S^{-1}$ is the frame operator of the dual frame $\tilde{f}$. Consequently, $f$ is the dual frame of $\tilde{f}$, so that for all $\phi\in H$, \begin{equation} \phi = \int_X\brak{\phi, \tilde{f}(x)} f(x)\,d\mu(x) = \int_X\brak{\phi, S^{-1}f(x)} f(x)\,d\mu(x). \end{equation} It is important to note, however, that there are dual frames for $f$ other than the canonical dual. Also, in what follows, we will often use a subscript of $H$ to denote inner products or norms with respect to the initial Hilbert space $H$.
nodes.statement_short: Duality is reciprocal with frame operator $S^{-1}$, and the canonical dual is not the only dual.

nodes.name: $F$ has uniformly bounded elements and $F_0$ is non-empty
nodes.statement: Note that $F$ is restricted to frames whose frame elements have uniformly bounded norms. Moreover, since $H$ is separable, it follows that $F_0$ is non-empty. That is, $H$ has at least one Parseval frame.

nodes.name: A fiber bundle is locally a product space
nodes.statement: Thus, a fiber bundle is simply a space that is locally a product space. Every product space $E = B\times E_1$ is a fiber bundle with base space either $B$ or $E_1$.

nodes.name: Continuity of $\zeta^{-1}$ is what remains
nodes.statement: In particular, $F$ is in one-one correspondence with $F_1\times\Fbar_0$. But to show $F$ is a fiber bundle, we also require continuity. In particular, for $F$ to be a fiber bundle with base space $\Fbar_0$, the projection $\sigma\circ T = \pi_1\circ\zeta^{-1}$ mapping $F$ onto $\Fbar_0$ must be continuous. Since $\pi_1$ is continuous, it suffices to have $\zeta^{-1}$ be continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Only continuity of $\zeta^{-1}$ is still needed for the bundle structure.

nodes.name: $\GL(H)$ is independent of the index set
nodes.statement: Although typically the group $\GL(H)$ is quite large, it is nonetheless independent of the indexing set $X$.  Thus, Theorem \ref{FiberBundle} is a description of the structure created by frames as maps from $X$ into $H.$   We believe that it has the potential to produce many applications and future directions of study.
nodes.statement_short: The structure group does not depend on $X$, so the main theorem describes frames purely as maps $X\to H$.

nodes.name: The base space arises from unitaries on the larger space
nodes.statement: The above example reveals that the base space $\Fbar_0$ can be obtained by the action of unitary operators $V^*$ on the frame $T$. Note that the operators $V^*$ do not act on the space $\CC^m$ that the frame spans but rather the possibly larger space $\CC^n$.

nodes.name: Future work: moving between fibers and continuous frames
nodes.statement: In the next paper, we extend this idea to show how the elements of a base space $\Fbar_0$ are connected to one another and therefore how one can ``move'' between fibers in a fiber bundle of frames. We also do this in the case of $X$ being non-countable, with applications to special classes of continuous frames such as coherent states, Gabor Frames, and wavelets.

nodes.name: Future work: reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and applications
nodes.statement: We will reveal the structure of $\Fbar_0$ by combining the results obtained in this paper with the structure of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, which are Hilbert spaces in which a function can be evaluated (or reproduced) by integrating it against a kernel function. If the kernel satisfies a certain condition, then this reproducing property is equivalent to the reconstruction property of frames \cite{ali2014coherent}. The connection of frames to reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces has applications to machine learning. In particular, because frames are more general than bases, then frames can be used to construct a variety of kernel functions for use in algorithms such as support vector machines \cite{rakotomamonjy2005frames}.
nodes.statement_short: Planned continuation: link $\Fbar_0$ to reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, with machine-learning applications.

nodes.name: Organization of the paper
nodes.statement: The paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we begin by reviewing the definition and basic properties of frames important to this paper. In section 3, we show that the set of all frames on a Hilbert space can be fibrated into orbits of a certain group action, thereby reducing the study of frames to only Parseval frames. In section 4, we establish the fiber bundle structure of the collection of all Parseval frames over a Hilbert space corresponding to a given index set $X$.   In section 5, we provide some basic examples  of this fiber bundle structure along with some possible applications and future directions.  In subsequent papers, we extend the ideas in this first paper to Gabor frames and the discretization problem.

nodes.name: Frames depend nonlinearly on the index
nodes.statement: As these examples illustrate, the richness of the structure of frames in general and Parseval frames in particular is due to a dependence on an index $x$ that does not change linearly with respect to $H$ itself. However, these examples also illustrate that frames are related to transformations that are linear in a larger vector space containing $H.$

nodes.name: Motivation for a top-down approach
nodes.statement: The examples above and the characterization of the finite dimensional cases implies the desirability of a top down approach to frames.  In particular, we use orbit spaces and fiber bundles both to establish the central importance of Parseval frames and to indicate how the structure of the set of all Parseval frames over a Hilbert space can be effectively represented and studied.

nodes.name: Frame operators live in $\GL^+(H)$
nodes.statement: Because frame operators are elements of $\GL^+(H)$, the above proposition will be useful in subsequent discussions of frame operators.

nodes.name: Toward indexing orbits by Parseval frames
nodes.statement: Therefore, every frame can be linearly transformed into a Parseval frame. But we would like this transformation to be unique in some sense. In particular, we would like to index the orbits in $F/\GL(H)$ by a set of Parseval frames. We must therefore determine how the Parseval frames in a common orbit in $F/\GL(H)$ are related. We recall that $F_0\subset F$ is the space of Parseval frames and consider the action of $U(H)$ on $F_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Motivates finding how Parseval frames in one orbit relate, so that $\Fbar_0$ can index orbits.
